sentences.text: Under certain circumstances, the Public Guardian may appoint suitable third parties, like social workers or medical care providers as professional deputies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: The Mental Capacity Act, however, does not empower the Public Guardian to intervene directly if a senior loses his or her mental capacity and has no viable person who can be appointed as a deputy to make decisions and manage matters on his or her behalf.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: This could result in vulnerable seniors failing to get the support or timely intervention they need, even with many willing helping hands in the community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: I ask if the Government will consider reviewing the Mental Capacity Act and empowering the Public Guardian to intervene directly in such cases?

sections.label: Australia Aged Care Act 2024
sections.summary: Australia's rights-based Aged Care Act 2024 came into force on 1 November 2025, focusing on seniors' rights, needs and personal choices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Interestingly, Australia also recently enacted the rights-based Aged Care Act 2024 which came into force on 1 November 2025 with a focus on empowering seniors to uphold their rights, needs and personal choices in their aged care.

sections.label: Value of unpaid caregiving
sections.summary: The World Economic Forum estimates global unpaid care compensation at about $11 trillion, and a 2024 Duke-NUS study values informal senior caregiving at $1.28 billion yearly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The World Economic Forum estimates compensation of unpaid care labour globally to be in the tune of roughly $11 trillion – 9% of global GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Closer to home, a 2024 Duke-National University of Singapore (NUS) study revealed that informal caregiving for our seniors aged 75 and above is worth $1.28 billion annually, an equivalent to 11% of our total Government expenditure on healthcare, which is today's second after defence.

sections.label: Seniors-led tier in SG Partnerships Fund
sections.summary: Proposes a seniors-led tier in the SG Partnerships Fund giving higher funding to initiatives led and joined by people above 60.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It is heartening to see the expansion of the SG Partnerships Fund, but we can be bolder.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I propose a specific seniors-led tier within this fund offering higher funding for ground-up initiatives led and participated by those above 60.

sections.label: Toa Payoh rental flat occupancy
sections.summary: Notes 17 rental blocks in Toa Payoh Central and a Parliamentary reply that median occupants in two-room rental flats is four.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In Toa Payoh, we have 17 rental blocks in Toa Payoh Central.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I noted in a Parliamentary Question reply this week that the median number of occupants in a two-room rental flat is four.

sections.label: Income and wealth inequality
sections.summary: States income inequality is at its lowest on record while wealth inequality has widened.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Our income inequality is at its lowest on record, but the more insidious wealth inequality has widened.

sections.label: Funding paid caregiving leave
sections.summary: Cites a $15.1 billion surplus as fiscal capacity to fund paid parent or elder caregiving leave, as childcare leave supports parents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: With a $15.1 billion surplus, we have the fiscal capacity to do exactly that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Caregivers often torn between being at work and the bedside, just as childcare leave supports the role of a parent, we must fund paid parent or elder caregiving leave.

sections.label: Upskilling foreign domestic workers
sections.summary: Notes foreign domestic workers are not required to have senior care qualifications and proposes subsidising geriatric and palliative care upskilling.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: While staff in senior care centres uphold basic care and nursing competencies, yet when those same seniors requiring specialised care return home at night and on weekends, we do not require our foreign domestic workers to have these similar qualifications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: We should subsidise upskilling specialised in geriatric and palliative care.

sections.label: Support for larger families
sections.summary: Calls for increased direct tiered support for families with three or more children to keep large families a strength, not household debt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: If demography is destiny, and families are bucking the trend to hold up our TFR, we must increase direct tiered support for families with three or more children to ensure that the invisible infrastructure of a large family remains a source of strength rather than a driver of household debt.

sections.label: AI and human care
sections.summary: AI helps identify vulnerable groups, but humans must fill every node in the care network.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: What they "Mai lai" or do not want to come, is that kind of cold interaction that has only graphics on a machine, without human dialogue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: We must be clear: AI is the "ladder" that helps us identify vulnerable groups, but every node in the care network must be filled by humans.

sections.label: Manufacturing and services shares
sections.summary: Manufacturing contributed about 20% of GDP on average, declining from 14% in 2015 to about 12% today.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Over the last decade, the manufacturing sector has, on average, contributed about 20% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And it has declined – from 14% in 2015 to about 12% today.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Over that same period, employment in exportable services – areas like finance, information technology (IT) and professional services – has grown as we diversified our economy.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Yet, taken together, the manufacturing, finance, IT and professional services segments of our economy account for just around 30% of employment.

sections.label: Skills frameworks and salaries
sections.summary: Skills frameworks were put in place, and salaries were increased for public healthcare and Government-supported preschool workers.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have put in place skills frameworks to articulate competencies, enable skills upgrading and support structured progression in these areas.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have increased salaries for workers in public healthcare institutions and Government-supported preschools.

sections.label: F&B and retail declines
sections.summary: Between 2019 and 2024, figures fell from 26% to 17% for F&B and from 30% to 26% for retail.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Between 2019 and 2024, they fell from 26% to 17% for the F&B sector; and from 30% to 26% for the retail sector.

sections.label: Progressive wages and foreign manpower
sections.summary: The Progressive Wage Credit Scheme is enhanced and extended, and the Dependency Ratio Ceiling cannot be relaxed.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is the right thing to do – to uplift incomes, strengthen dignity in work and narrow wage gaps.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And at the same time, to support businesses through the transition, we introduced the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme and, in this Budget, we are enhancing the Scheme and extending it for another two years.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Mr Mark Lee asked for more leeway for SMEs to hire foreign workers.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We cannot relax the Dependency Ratio Ceiling (DRC).

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Doing so will encourage excessive reliance on foreign manpower and weaken our Singaporean core.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But we will consider calibrated ways to provide more flexibility, like expanding the sources from which businesses can hire Work Permit holders, for certain types of occupations where genuine shortages exist.

sections.label: AI tools and expansion
sections.summary: With Government support, it is developing AI tools to analyse customer data and shopping behaviour, and employs 150 people.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And with Government support, it is developing AI tools to analyse customer data and shopping behaviour, so as to enable more personalised product recommendations.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And it now employs 150 people and is making plans to expand into ASEAN.

sections.label: Employment and PMET vacancies
sections.summary: Permanent employees reached nearly 91%, vacancies outnumber jobseekers, and over 40% of openings are entry-level PMET roles.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The proportion of permanent employees has risen to a record high of nearly 91%, with gains across most sectors.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Vacancies continue to outnumber jobseekers and over 40% of openings are entry-level professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMET) roles, indicating still healthy demand for young graduates.

sections.label: No jobless growth pledge
sections.summary: The strategy is that Singapore will not have jobless growth, after better than expected 5% growth last year.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is our assurance and that is why our strategy going ahead is clear.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We will not have jobless growth in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: That is how we give every Singaporean confidence to progress in the future.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We achieved better than expected growth of 5% last year.

sections.label: Rate rose then fell
sections.summary: In Singapore it rose to more than 6% in 2022 and has since come down to 0.9% last year.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In Singapore, it rose to more than 6% in 2022 and it has since come down to 0.9% last year.

sections.label: More for seniors and retirees
sections.summary: More is given to those with greater needs and to seniors, especially retirees not working on fixed incomes.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Essentially, we give more to those with greater needs and we give more to seniors, especially our retirees, as they are not working and have to cope with higher prices on fixed incomes.

sections.label: One-off versus structural Budget
sections.summary: About 5% of the overall Budget is for one-off measures in FY2025 and FY2026, with 95% for longer-term structural schemes.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Because the facts are only about 5% of our overall Budget is for one-off measures – that was so in FY2025 and it is so in FY2026.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The remaining 95%, the overwhelming share, is for longer-term and structural schemes.

sections.label: Retirees and income versus inflation
sections.summary: Retirees face greater impact as they are not working, so the Budget provides more for them; incomes rose faster than inflation over the past decade.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: He highlighted the concerns among seniors and, indeed, one group that will face greater impact is retirees because they are not working and that is why we provide more for them in the Budget.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But when we look at data at both the household and the individual worker levels – household and workers – in fact, incomes have risen faster than inflation over the past decade, across the entire income distribution.

sections.label: Healthcare spending share of income
sections.summary: Singaporeans are spending a larger share of their income on healthcare and health insurance.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Singaporeans are spending a larger share of their income on healthcare and health insurance.

sections.label: AV and PCHI indicators
sections.summary: AV and PCHI are practical and effective indicators, but no measure is perfect and criteria will continue to be refined, especially for seniors.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: AV and PCHI are practical and effective indicators.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: But no measure is perfect and we will continue refining our criteria, especially when it comes to support for seniors.

sections.label: Lowest quintile household net wealth
sections.summary: Households in the lowest quintile have average net wealth of nearly $300,000, which is a meaningful foundation.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Today, households in the lowest quintile have average net wealth of nearly $300,000 – that is a meaningful foundation.

sections.label: CPFIS investment returns
sections.summary: From 2016 to 2024, about half of CPFIS-OA investors earned over 4%, while around three in four CPFIS-SA investors made 4% or less.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: From 2016 to 2024, while a majority of CPFIS-OA investors earned above 2.5% per annum, only about half achieved returns of more than 4%; this is for OA.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For CPFIS-SA investors, the results were even more sobering – around three in four made 4% or less per annum.

sections.label: CPF Board scheme rollout
sections.summary: The CPF Board will engage the industry next month to call for expressions of interest and aims to roll out the scheme in the first half of 2028.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The CPF Board will be engaging the industry next month to call for expressions of interest.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The CPF Board is working towards rolling out the scheme in the first half of 2028, but if we can do this earlier, we will.

sections.label: ComLink+ families in rental housing
sections.summary: About 11,000 families are on ComLink+, most of whom are in rental housing.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Mr Abdul Muhaimin asked about this particular issue of ComLink+.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: There are, today, about 11,000 families on ComLink+, most are in rental housing.

sections.label: Large Families Scheme and spending
sections.summary: Parents can receive up to $48,000 for a third or fourth child, and marriage and parenthood expenditure rose from $4 billion to $7 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In fact, we have taken significant steps on both fronts recently.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And with the Large Families Scheme, parents can now receive up to $48,000 for their third or fourth child, and even more for the fifth or subsequent child.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: As a result of the recent enhancements, our expenditure on marriage and parenthood initiatives has increased – from $4 billion in FY2020 to $7 billion in this Budget.

sections.label: Healthcare funding and tax moves
sections.summary: Healthcare was estimated to need 0.6% to 1.2% of GDP; property, luxury car and top income taxes rose, and the NIRC proposal was rejected.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We had estimated that healthcare alone would require additional funding of 0.6% to 1.2% of GDP and this would happen in the second half of this decade, which we are in right now.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We raised property taxes and motor vehicle taxes for luxury cars.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have increased the top marginal personal income tax rates.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The WP had suggested raising the maximum Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) we can use in the Annual Budget from 50% to 60%.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We did not agree with that proposal, because the NIRC framework was carefully designed to safeguard intergenerational equity.

sections.label: GST to fund healthcare
sections.summary: The GST was the only broad-based and sustainable option to fund rising healthcare needs while preserving the reserves framework.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: In the end, the GST was the only broad-based and sustainable option to fund rising healthcare needs, while preserving our reserves framework.

sections.label: Corporate tax collections
sections.summary: Based on strong corporate tax collections so far, the further increase from top-up taxes could be significant.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Based on the strong corporate tax collections so far – and that is pre top-up taxes – our initial sense is that the further increase from the top-up taxes could be significant.

sections.label: Spending, fiscal position, GST
sections.summary: Spending is likely to exceed 20% of GDP well before 2030, the fiscal position is expected to remain healthy, and there will be no further GST increases until at least 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And we expect our needs to rise even more for the coming years, in this term of Government.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, Government spending is likely to exceed 20% of GDP well before 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: At this juncture, if circumstances remain broadly stable and without any further major revenue moves, we expect our fiscal position during this term of Government to remain healthy.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We have already said that there will be no further GST increases until at least 2030.

sections.label: Updated medium-term projections
sections.summary: Updated medium-term projections extending to 2035 will be published by next year.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: With updated revenue and expenditure developments, these projections will need to be refreshed.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, we will publish updated medium-term projections extending to 2035 by next year.

sections.label: Vehicle tax changes timing
sections.summary: Vehicle tax changes were implemented immediately to prevent a rush-to-market, in response to a question on the Preferential Additional Registration Fee rebate timing.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Ms Diana Pang asked about the timing of the changes to the Preferential Additional Registration Fee rebate.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: We implemented the vehicle tax changes immediately to prevent a rush-to-market.

sections.label: Resident workers income tax
sections.summary: With progressive tax rates, reliefs and rebates, about one in three resident workers pay no personal income tax, and about eight in 10 of those who do have an effective rate under 6%.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: When taken together with our progressive tax rates, tax reliefs and rebates, currently about one in three resident workers pay no personal income tax.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Among those who do, about eight in 10 have an effective tax rate of less than 6%.

sections.label: Revenue and investment income
sections.summary: Singapore's revenue includes significant investment income from reserves, so excluding Net Investment Returns Contribution, expenditure exceeds revenue.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And in Singapore's case, revenue includes significant investment income from our reserves, not just taxes collected from businesses and households.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: So, if you exclude Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC), expenditure exceeds revenue.

sections.label: Top quintile tax benefits
sections.summary: For every dollar of tax paid by the top quintile, they receive 20 cents in benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For every dollar of tax paid by the top quintile, they receive 20 cents in benefits.

sections.label: Tax benefits by quintile
sections.summary: A dollar of tax can return more, $2 in benefits, and the bottom quintile gets $7 in benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: A dollar of tax, you can get back more, $2 in benefits.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: And the bottom quintile gets $7 in benefits.

sections.label: RIE 2030 accountability
sections.summary: It dives into the RIE domains, showing accountability for how the $37 billion committed to RIE 2030 will be expended and how Singaporean jobs will be enhanced.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It just dives straight into the RIE domains.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And this is an example of, I think, the sort of accountability people are actually interested in looking at – how or where the $37 billion, which was committed to RIE 2030, how it will be expended, how Singaporean jobs will be enhanced and what opportunities there would be for Singaporean, to say nothing of the budgetary issues.

sections.label: Ministries sharing resource information
sections.summary: Ministries are being asked to share more information on resource use and outcomes, including in RIE.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I see the value of getting Ministries to put out more information, to share more about how their resources are being used and what outcomes they have achieved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And so, as I have committed in this Budget, or in the speech just now, we are getting Ministries to do more, certainly in the area of RIE as well.

sections.label: Pillar Two revenue downside risk
sections.summary: Revenue upsides were expected, but Pillar Two implementation was uncertain, so downside risk has now fallen.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And that would give upsides to revenue, but we were not sure at that time whether Pillar Two would be implemented.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, the downside risk has come down, at least for now.

sections.label: Pillar Two domestic top-up tax
sections.summary: Pillar Two has broad consensus, and jurisdictions including Singapore have implemented their domestic top-up tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Pillar Two has had broad-based consensus and therefore, jurisdiction after jurisdiction have been implementing their version of a domestic top-up tax, and we have too.

sections.label: Competitive landscape revenue and spending
sections.summary: Domestic top-up tax revenue is more assured, but more economic spending is likely needed to stay competitive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is the reality of the competitive landscape.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, the revenue upside is more assured, in terms of the domestic top-up tax, but at the same time, we are very likely to also have to spend more on the economic front to stay competitive.

sections.label: Rental rates and no caps
sections.summary: Rental rates have moved with economic fundamentals and remain stable, so no rental caps are envisaged.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, as I mentioned just now, at the macro level, rental rates have moved in line with economic fundamentals – lower than GDP growth, lower than inflation rates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There will always be a distribution of rental increases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But overall, the situation remains stable, so we do not envisage imposing rental caps, particularly since at the macro level, the situation remains stable.

sections.label: Services DRC kept whole
sections.summary: The DRC is lower than construction, but F&B is not carved out because F&B and other services are hard to distinguish.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The DRC is lower than construction, but we prefer not to carve out something separate for F&B, because it is really very hard to distinguish between F&B as a service and the other service industries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Once you make the DRC for F&B lower, you can be sure there will be many F&B foreign workers in Singapore doing non-F&B jobs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It is very hard to enforce because they are all service-related.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, we rather keep services DRC as a whole, where it is.

sections.label: Economic assumptions for fiscal projections
sections.summary: The speaker says economic assumptions underpinning fiscal projections will be provided.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: First, yes, we will provide the economic assumptions underpinning our fiscal projections.

sections.label: Personal income tax thresholds
sections.summary: Suggestions on personal income tax thresholds will be taken on board in regular fiscal reviews.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Thirdly, on the personal income tax thresholds, as I said just now, we will take on board these suggestions as part of our regular fiscal reviews.

sections.label: Rental caps and interventions
sections.summary: Rental caps are not thought to work, but interventions will consider different circumstances such as supply shortages or sharp rental increases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We know that this happens, but the interventions and the way we help will have to take into account the different considerations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We do not think rental caps will work, but for example, if we understand better a particular situation where there has been very sharp increase in rental for that location, it could be a supply source shortage, there could be specific circumstances linked to that area.

sections.label: Global marketplace trends and workers
sections.summary: The speaker says they are alive to the risk and will consider additional levers and steps if global marketplace trends move that way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are, as I said in my speech, I did not highlight that in such terms, but that is the risk we are very much alive to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And if the trends in the marketplace globally are moving in that direction, well, we will have to consider what additional levers, what steps to take, how we ensure that workers benefit from growth.

sections.label: Fiscal space for growth
sections.summary: The speaker confirms openness to using fiscal space and resources for growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On the question around our openness to using fiscal space and resources for growth, yes, of course we are.

sections.label: Structural levers versus one-off decisions
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether surpluses make structural levers and interventions better than deciding one-off year after year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To me, the question is really, as I have shared in my speech, in light of our surpluses, are we then better off to put in place the structural levers and interventions, rather than having to decide on these on a one-off basis year after year?

sections.label: Timeline for wealth tax recommendations
sections.summary: Asks whether the Prime Minister gave MOF a timeline for recommendations on taxing wealth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Just wondering if the Prime Minister has given the MOF team perhaps a timeline as to when recommendations may be put forth to address some of the issues that were brought up, specifically when it comes to the taxing of wealth.

sections.label: Occasional Paper and fiscal reviews
sections.summary: States the Occasional Paper comes next year and fiscal reviews are regular, with no specific timeline.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The Occasional Paper that we are putting out will be done by next year, but the fiscal reviews that we do on the policy front, that happens on a regular basis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There is no specific timeline for this because we are always on a continuing basis, reviewing and updating our policies.

sections.label: Ambitious coming policy review
sections.summary: Says each move pushed the boundary and the coming review will be even more ambitious.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have pushed the boundary each time in terms of the moves we made.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And in this coming review we will be even more ambitious.

sections.label: Decarbonisation and clean energy sources
sections.summary: Says the solution is accelerating decarbonisation and harnessing more clean energy sources, including imports, hydrogen and civilian nuclear energy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I think Mr Dennis Tan had also spoken about this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are trying our best to manage this and the solution for us at the end of the day is to accelerate our efforts on decarbonisation to be able to harness even more clean energy sources than the limited sources we have today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The new sources may not materialise in the short term.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are working on multiple fronts, including importing clean energy from outside Singapore, pursuing ideas like hydrogen, as well as civilian nuclear energy.

sections.label: Managing technology transition for workers
sections.summary: Assures careful management of technology transition with union engagement, retraining and pacing, and notes 1% of GDP for R&D.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The assurance I gave then and I give now is that we will manage this very carefully.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We already have very close engagement with the unions and drivers, and as we introduce these new technologies, we will pace the transition in a way that ensures that we are also able to retrain workers if jobs are impacted and make sure that the transition and the introduction of technologies do not adversely impact our workers.

sentences.speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Prime Minister mentioned in his Budget speech that 1% of the GDP is dedicated to R&D expenses, commonly known as the gross expenditure on R&D (GERD).

sections.label: National Technology Plan to RIE2030 funding
sections.summary: States that since 1991, from the first National Technology Plan to RIE2030, about $125 billion nominal was committed, with few visible commercial outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: First, since 1991, the first National Technology Plan to RIE2030, the nominal amount committed is about $125 billion, of which I think there are indeed few visible commercial outcomes.

sections.label: Policy investment bank function
sections.summary: A speaker asks whether a policy investment bank function will be considered or reconstituted, noting it has been missing since Mdm Ho Ching took over Temasek in 2002.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
sentences.text: My second clarification is whether he will consider putting on a policy investment bank function or, rather, reconstituting it, given that it has been missing since Mdm Ho Ching took over Temasek in 2002.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It is not just on the basis of a company getting IPO success.

sections.label: Wider economy and R&D outcomes
sections.summary: The passage states there are outcomes for the wider economy, raised incomes, and business expenditure on R&D.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There are outcomes to the wider economy and incomes that are raised.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There are outcomes with regards to business expenditure on R&D, which we have talked about just now.

sections.label: Mr Tiong's one-sided views
sections.summary: A speaker says Mr Tiong's views were one-sided but agrees with his broad principle that the system can be risk-averse and more can be done on value capture.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why I said just now that the views that Mr Tiong had highlighted were rather one-sided.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I do agree with Mr Tiong though, about what he said about the broad principle that sometimes the system can be risk-averse, that there are ways to do more in terms of value capture.

sections.label: Temasek's commercial mandate
sections.summary: Temasek was clear from the start about its mandate: commercial, not national service, focused on commercial outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Temasek, when it started, was always very clear about its mandate from the very beginning – commercial, not doing national service, focused on commercial outcomes.

sections.label: Prime Minister on jobless growth
sections.summary: The passage concerns the Prime Minister's comment on no jobless growth.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The second one is on the Prime Minister's comment on no jobless growth.

sections.label: Jobless growth and vulnerable groups
sections.summary: Social support has been strengthened with Jobseeker Support and SkillsFuture, and AI's impact on vulnerable workers and seniors will be monitored and reviewed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Second, on jobless growth and the concerns that vulnerable groups may have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why we have progressively strengthened our social support system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We have put in place Jobseeker Support, we are strengthening SkillsFuture and we will continue to monitor this segment very closely and the impact that AI may have on vulnerable and disadvantaged workers, on seniors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We will continually review and strengthen our support mechanisms.

sections.label: Education support and exam anxiety
sections.summary: Education is a key agenda item for this term, focusing on helping disadvantaged groups and addressing concerns about high-stakes exams.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, many Members spoke about education during the debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I did not really touch on it as a topic in the round-up speech, but we have this as one of the key items on our agenda for this term of Government, looking at how we can especially help disadvantaged groups level up in our education system, focusing on those with less resources, those with different start points, making sure that more support is given to them, but at the same time addressing the other concern too, which many Members spoke about – the concerns about high-stakes exams, the anxiety about the arms race that parents and students are feeling.

sections.label: Surpluses exceeding original estimates
sections.summary: For 18 of 20 years, actual surpluses consistently exceeded original estimates by significant margins.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For 18 of these 20 years, the actual surpluses have consistently exceeded original estimates by significant margins.

sections.label: Singapore's long-term human potential
sections.summary: Singapore's long-term potential depends on being able to maximise its human potential.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In fact, I would say the long-term potential of Singapore, how far we go really depends on us being able to maximise our human potential.

sections.label: SkillsFuture and social compact
sections.summary: Learning may need refreshing years after graduation, so SkillsFuture is a key pillar of the social compact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Whatever you have learned in school or from tertiary levels of education may very well need a refresh and an update a few years later after you graduate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And that is again why we are investing significantly in SkillsFuture and we have made it a key pillar in our social compact.

sections.label: Retirees and rising cost of living
sections.summary: Rising incomes guard against cost-of-living increases, but half a million retirees do not experience rising incomes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Specifically, he acknowledged that rising incomes are the best way to guard against increases in the cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: But he also acknowledged that for the half a million retirees in Singapore, they do not experience these rising incomes when the cost of living increases.

sections.label: Monitoring cost of living for retirees
sections.summary: Cost of living will continue to be monitored, with retirees facing the biggest concerns as they lack incomes and wage increases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: To answer the question, we will continue to monitor cost of living across all segments of society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: We are very mindful that retirees will face potentially the biggest concerns because they do not have incomes, they will not benefit from wage increases and the cost-of-living pressures would be felt more acutely by this segment.

sections.label: Retraining workforce and SkillsFuture revamp
sections.summary: The speaker calls for a fundamental revamp of SkillsFuture and retraining the workforce every 10 years to counter shorter economic cycles and AI.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
sentences.text: In my speech, I asked to help our young seniors stay relevant and employable for the long term.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
sentences.text: I call for more fundamental revamp of the SkillsFuture and to retrain our workforce every 10 years or so, to counter the shorter economic cycles and the impact of AI.

sections.label: Wage plateau and mid-career support
sections.summary: Wage increases plateau after a while, so schemes like Level-Up for those above 40 exist, and the SSG-WSG merger may strengthen mid-career support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Wage increases tend to be higher when you are younger and then, after a while, it starts to plateau off.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why we have already put in place schemes, like Level-Up for those above 40.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And we will continue to see how we can strengthen support for mid-career, young seniors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And with the merger of SSG and WSG, I am sure we can do more.

sections.label: Economic growth funds social policies
sections.summary: Policies and schemes need resources, which come from good economic growth, so the fundamentals of a dynamic, growing economy must be maintained.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Policies take time, new schemes take resources and importantly, let us be very mindful, we are able to talk about all of these things and all the good things we can do because our economy has done well, because we have good growth and now, we are in a position with the resources to act decisively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: If these foundations are not present, we would be scrambling, we would be having a very different conversation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, let us also be mindful of the fundamentals – keep growth, keep our economy growing, keep on ensuring a dynamic vibrant economy, good growth and generate the resources we need in order to take care of all the different segments of society.
